title: Commission tiers with nested IF
summary: Look up a sales rate from a tier table by placing one IF inside another.

blocks.text: The Eldoret store pays its sales reps a commission on a sliding scale. The more a rep sells in the month, the higher the rate. HR sends you the tier table and the month's sales, and wants every rep's rate by lunchtime.
One IF can only choose between two results. A tier table has three, so you place an IF inside another IF. This is called a nested IF. It is the classic way to look up a rate from a table of bands.

items: Objective: return a rate from a tier table using nested IF and absolute references.
You pass the mission at 75% or more in the Assessment.

blocks.text: A rep gets the rate of the highest tier they have reached. Selling 87,500 has reached the 50,000 tier but not the 100,000 tier, so the rate is 4%.

Read it from the outside in. If sales (B2) have reached the top tier in F4, return its rate in G4. Otherwise, run the second IF: if they have reached the middle tier in F3, return G3. If neither is true, the rep is in the first tier, so return G2.
Worked example. Sales are 87,500. Is 87,500 >= 100,000? No, so Excel moves to the inner IF. Is 87,500 >= 50,000? Yes, so the answer is the middle rate, 4%.
Always test the highest tier first. If you test the lowest tier first, every rep passes it and everyone gets 2%.

Use >= (at or above), because a rep who sells exactly 50,000 has reached the 50,000 tier. The $ signs in $F$4 lock the tier table, so the formula still points at the table when you copy it down to the next rep. B2 has no $ signs on purpose: it must move to B3, B4 and so on.
Tip: a table with n tiers needs n - 1 IF functions. The last tier needs no test, because it is what remains. Also note that the simulator stores 4% as 0.04, because it has no number formats.
Four questions on nested IF and tier tables. Type numbers without commas, for example 3500.

items: A nested IF places one IF inside the value_if_false part of another, so one formula can choose between three or more results.
Test the highest tier first and use >= so the boundary amount belongs to the higher tier.
Point at the tier table with $ signs (absolute references) so the table stays fixed when you copy the formula down.
A table with n tiers needs n - 1 IF functions.

items.prompt: Using the tier table in the training (2% from 0, 4% from 50,000, 6% from 100,000), a rep sells KES 64,000. How much commission, in KES, does the rep earn?
A rep sells exactly KES 50,000. With the formula =IF(B2>=$F$4,$G$4,IF(B2>=$F$3,$G$3,$G$2)), which rate does the rep get?

options.label: An error, because 50,000 is on the boundary

items.prompt: Why does the formula test the highest tier (>= $F$4) first?

options.label: IF stops at the first test that is TRUE, so testing the lowest tier first would give everyone the lowest rate
Excel calculates the largest numbers faster
Excel only accepts tiers listed from highest to lowest
The order makes no difference to the result
